item.title: Stage-Resolved EBV-Induced B-Cell Programs Across CNS Selection and Multiple Sclerosis Compartments
item.description: arXiv:2611.14524v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) is implicated in multiple sclerosis (MS), but whether EBV-conditioned B cells retain stable transcriptional programs after CNS selection remains uncertain. We reanalyzed datasets spanning experimental EBV infection, CNS-homing B cells in humanized mice, early-MS blood, and paired human CSF and blood. A frozen EBV-induced B-cell factor (F12) was transferred without outcome-driven modification and evaluated using anatomical, sequencing-depth, metabolic, coherence-matched, lineage, and exposure controls. F12 did not predict MS activity (AUC=0.487; p=0.489) and was lower in CSF in nine evaluable participants (mean difference -0.0560; coherence-matched p=0.015). It also remained lower in brain than spleen in all five EBV-exposed mice after matched-depth rarefaction (p=0.0313) and coherence-matched calibration (p=0.0225). The splenic TBX21+CXCR3+ transcriptional gate did not reliably represent the state of anatomically selected brain B cells. An enriched 287-gene cross-system bridge lacked B-lineage and EBV-exposure specificity. In human CSF, an early EBV-associated program was depleted (-0.0492; p=0.0197), whereas latency-III and lymphoblastoid cell line-like programs increased (+0.0666; p=0.0092 and +0.0148; p=0.0096, respectively). Opposite early and late program directions persisted after removing shared genes. No external program met the prespecified prospective criterion. These findings support stage- and compartment-dependent remodeling of EBV-associated B-cell transcription rather than persistence of a stable RNA signature. They distinguish cellular trafficking from transcriptional-state preservation and show that cross-system molecular resemblance alone cannot establish ancestry. EBV-directed biomarker studies should integrate host transcription with virologic, clonotypic, antigen-specific, epigenetic, and longitudinal evidence.
item.dc:creator: Hasan Jamil, Alexander Gow

item.title: AVA: Agentic Variant Adjudication for Automated, Auditable Read-Level Review in Cancer Diagnostic Sequencing
item.description: arXiv:2611.14560v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identifying a tumor's DNA mutations is central to cancer diagnosis and treatment, but distinguishing genuine mutations from sequencing artifacts is error-prone. In practice, genuine mutations are identified using fixed variant-allele-frequency (VAF) and depth thresholds which cannot separate artifacts from genuine mutations in the borderline low-VAF zone where they overlap. A laboratory specialist must manually inspect the read-level sequencing data, a slow step that has high inter-rater variability and causes diagnosis delays. We present AVA: Agentic Variant Adjudication; an agentic framework that automates this read-level inspection with subagents that reason over evidence, generate investigative code, and return a real-or-artifact adjudications with an auditable reasoning trace all without training on existing data. On both the SEQC2 DNA-seq benchmark and patient RNA-seq data, restricted to a subsample of borderline variants where thresholds fail, both closed-source (Claude Sonnet 5) and open-weight (GLM 5.3 Flash and Gemma 4 31b) agents outperform the best achievable VAF/depth thresholds. Ultimately, AVA is suited for privacy-constrained clinical deployment, since the framework can run on locally deployed open-weight models with descriptive reasoning traces to keep specialists in the loop.
item.dc:creator: Caleb Chin, Sidharth Gupta, Arun K Anguraj Vadivel, Robert Siddaway, Siddharth Arya, Arianna He, Peter Zhukovsky, Cynthia Hawkins

item.title: Deep learning-guided discovery reveals the diversity and mutational potential of environmental beta-lactamases
item.description: arXiv:2611.14568v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Beta-lactamases are a major mechanism of bacterial resistance to beta-lactam antibiotics; however, their functional diversity and mutational potential in environmental microbial communities remain partially understood. This study aimed to characterize environmental beta-lactamase diversity and investigate how sequence variation influences antibiotic resistance. By integrating protein language model (PLMs) with ensemble learning, we identified more than 46,000 putative beta-lactamases across all four Ambler classes from environmental metagenomes, widely distributed across diverse habitats, with distinct habitat-associated class compositions. The candidates sharing approximately 30% sequence identity with known beta-lactamases conferred resistance to multiple beta-lactam antibiotics when expressed in Escherichia coli. Combining inverse folding model with PLMs further identified mutations that altered resistance profiles, including substitutions that increased resistance to carbapenems. Predicted high-fitness sites exhibited greater natural sequence variability overall, with higher variability in wastewater-derived than ocean-derived enzymes. These findings reveal undercharacterized beta-lactamase diversity and substantial mutational flexibility in environmental microbiomes, providing a basis for investigating their potential contribution to the diversification of antibiotic resistance.
item.dc:creator: Liangjun Ge, Qiandi Gao, Haiming Xu, Zhiwei Qin, Heqian Zhang

item.title: MutAtlas: A PDB-Wide Energy-Guided Atlas of Protein Mutation Effects
item.description: arXiv:2611.16361v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Protein mutation effect prediction is fundamental to protein engineering and disease variant interpretation, yet experimentally measured mutation data remain accurate but extremely sparse. To provide scalable supplementary mutation signals, we construct a PDB-wide mutation augmentation dataset that exhaustively enumerates single-site substitutions on experimentally resolved protein structures and aligns mutation signals from physics-based energy models, protein language models, and inverse folding models. Large-scale analysis under a unified mutation preference representation reveals substantial differences in the consistency, concentration, and substitution patterns of mutation distributions across models, indicating that disagreement is pervasive and reflects conflicting inductive biases rather than random noise. Motivated by these observations, we propose an unsupervised multi-source mutation preference distillation framework that learns from relative mutation preferences while explicitly modeling cross-source disagreement. Without using any experimental mutation labels during training, our approach achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated zero-shot baselines and naive multi-source fusion strategies on ProteinGym. We release the dataset and evaluation pipeline to support reproducible studies of protein mutation effects.
item.dc:creator: Ruihan Guo, Chaoran Cheng, Zhanghan Ni, Neil He, Bangji Yang, Ge Liu

item.title: Designing Cell-Type-Specific Regulatory DNA with Guided Discrete Diffusion
item.description: arXiv:2604.20488v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: AI-driven design of DNA with cell-type-specific regulatory activity is broadly relevant for cell engineering and gene therapy. DNA elements such as promoters and enhancers have gene-regulatory functions that are defined by their DNA sequence and follow a characteristic regulatory grammar. Deep learning models can effectively predict DNA regulatory activity across cell types, but current generative methods often produce DNA sequences that deviate from the native regulatory grammar, increasing the risk of unexpected behavior and off-target effects in real-world applications. Here, we introduce DNA-CRAFT, a method for designing regulatory DNA with high predicted cell-type-specific activity while preserving naturalness. DNA-CRAFT formulates regulatory sequence design as a guided search over a generative model pre-trained on millions of naturally occurring regulatory elements from the human and mouse genomes. Our method enables targeted exploration of the DNA sequence space, efficient evaluation of candidate designs, and explicit suppression of unwanted activity. Across benchmarks spanning human cell lines and primary immune cells, DNA-CRAFT combines high predicted cell-type specificity with strong motif and sequence-composition adherence, achieving favorable results across the evaluated DNA design tasks.
item.dc:creator: Animesh Awasthi, Martin Stoll, Raphael Bednarsky, Moritz Schaefer, Christoph Bock

item.title: Navigating Selection Bias in Genome-wide Association Studies (GWAS)
item.description: arXiv:2611.09429v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Selection bias arises when inclusion in a genetic study depends on traits, or causes of traits, that are associated with genotype. It is present in volunteer-based biobanks, case-control designs and studies of disease progression, and genome-wide association study (GWAS) summary statistics from affected samples can propagate this bias into post-GWAS analyses, such as polygenic scores (PGS), Mendelian randomization (MR) and genetic correlation analyses. Despite broad potential impact of selection bias it is sometimes ignored in genetic studies. Many methods exist to detect and correct selection bias, but they rely on different assumptions and require specific data. We organise ten methods applicable to GWAS by the decisions an analyst faces: whether to diagnose or correct, which data are available (individual-level or summary-level), and which form of selection is operating (non-representative participation, case-control ascertainment, index events, sex-differential participation or survival to recruitment). For each method, we describe its principle, applicability, limitations and data requirements. A companion GitHub repository implements nine methods in R and prepares input for the external SPREG software. It provides worked examples using simulated data with known true effects for each form of selection. An interactive tool supports method selection. We conclude with open methodological challenges.
item.dc:creator: Ciarrah-Jane S Barry, Tahereh Gholipourshahraki, Zolt\'an Kutalik, Bjarni J Vilhj\'almsson, Esben Agerbo
